title: Optimisation of vertically mounted agrivoltaic systems
abstract: Agrivoltaic systems represent a key technology for reaching sustainable development goals, by reducing the competition of land used for food versus land used for electricity. Moreover, agrivoltaic systems are at the centre of the nexus between electricity production, crop production, and irrigation water savings. In this study, an optimisation model for vertically mounted agrivoltaic systems with bifacial photovoltaic modules is developed. The model combines three main sub-models: solar radiation and shadings, photovoltaics, and crop yield. Validation of the sub-models is performed showing good agreement with measured data and commercial software. The optimisation model is set as multi objective to explore the trade-offs between competing agrivoltaic key performance indicators. Oats and potatoes are used as reference crops in this study. The results show that the row distance between bifacial photovoltaic module structures significantly affects the photosynthetically active radiation distribution. The resulting crop yield of oats and potato is reduced by about 50% as row distance decreases from 20 m to 5 m. The implementation of an agrivoltaic system for the investigated crops at the chosen location shows a land equivalent ratio above 1.2, which justifies the use of the technology for reaching national sustainability goals.

## **1. Introduction**

At the end of 2019, the photovoltaic system capacity in Sweden was 698 MWp with a total estimated production of about 540 GWh that accounted for 0.41% of the total electricity supply (Lindahl et al., 2020). At the end of 2019, ground-mounted centralised _PV_ parks represented only 5% of the total grid-connected market in Sweden; nevertheless, as highlighted by Lindahl et al. (2020), this market segment has significantly increased in the last two years, and it is expected to increase in the coming years. This is also boosted by the Swedish government targets of 100% purely renewable-based power supply for 2040 (Government Offices of Sweden, 2021a) and net zero emissions of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere by 2045 (Government Offices of Sweden, 2021b). Despite the rapid development of the _PV_ sector in Sweden, _PV_ installations still suffer a major issue – system profitability. The profitability is threatened by low electricity prices, low annual solar irradiation, seasonality of solar radiation, and lower subsidies as compared to other southern European countries like Italy (D’Adamo et al., 2020, 2021). These aspects have been clearly discussed in a recently published study on _PV_ systems optimisation that covers all of

Sweden (Campana et al., 2020). New solutions and business models are required to make solar _PV_ systems, and in particular solar parks, more economically profitable to easily pursue the national targets of high renewable penetrations and net zero emissions. Traditionally, land-based _PV_ farms have increased the competition for land resources for food production (Nonhebel, 2005). Nevertheless, in recent years, researchers mostly from France, Germany, Japan, Italy, and the USA have proven that agrivoltaic systems, which are a combination of farm activities and _PV_ farms, can overcome the competition for land for food vs land for energy.

Agrivoltaic systems present several advantages over traditional ground-based PV systems and, by adopting a holistic approach, those advantages are cut across three different macro-areas: energy, food, and water. First, the combination of power and crop production can increase the economic benefits of the entire system. By combining synergies and revenues, the payback period of _PV_ systems can decrease, making ground-based _PV_ systems more attractive and thus easily supporting national renewable energy targets. Moreover, by combining farm activities, for instance irrigation and _PV_ production, the selfconsumption rate is higher, since commonly most of the agricultural activities are concentrated during those months with higher solar radiation and thus higher production. Higher self-consumption rates can lead to several benefits in the electricity grid by avoiding congestion and thus increasing revenues due to the mismatch between selling and buying prices for electricity. From a food and water perspective, agrivoltaic systems have the potential to lead to higher crop yields because the shade provided by optimally distributed _PV_ panels decreases the amount of water required by crops and increases soil moisture. This is of paramount importance, especially in the context of the negative effects that climate changes and weather extremes (i.e., increased temperatures, decreased precipitation, and drought) can have on crop yields.

A typical configuration of an agrivoltaic system consists in having the _PV_ modules installed at a height of 2–5 m above ground using suspended structures, to allow normal farm activities underneath. This concept was first introduced in the 1980s by Goetzberger and Zastrow (1982). Nevertheless, one of the first agrivoltaic experiments was conducted in France in 2013 by Marrou et al. (2013) using vegetables as the crop. The authors conducted an experiment with two shading levels equal to 50% and 70%, and observed a negligible change in the radiation conversion efficiency. The authors suggested that optimisation was required to find the best trade-off of _PV_ module densities for balancing food production and electricity production. In a previous work conducted by the same research group, it was proven through modelling that the combination of _PV_ modules and agriculture could lead to an increase in land productivity of 60–70% (Dupraz et al., 2011). More recently, Dinesh and Pearce (2016) have shown that an agrivoltaic system can increase a farm’s generated economic value by about 30% as compared to common practices in the USA. In 2017, in an experiment carried out in Heggelbach, the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems (2021) obtained a land-use efficiency of 160% as compared to the reference case of only crop production (100% land-use efficiency in producing food) or electricity production (100% land-use efficiency in producing electricity)

(land-use efficiency is defined as the percentage of land equivalent ratio [ _LER_ ] introduced in Section 2.7). In 2018, while a severe drought affected almost all of Europe, a land-use efficiency above 180% was achieved. The higher land-use efficiency in 2018 as compared to 2017 was due to the higher crop yield under the agrivoltaic system as compared to the ground control. This was achieved due to the lower water and temperature stresses on the crop under the agrivoltaic system. Amaducci et al. (2018) demonstrated that agrivoltaic systems with an optimal density of _PV_ modules can also increase crop yields, since they can maintain higher levels of soil moisture. The study is based on an extensive simulation approach on an agrivoltaic system installed in Northern Italy using 40 years’ climatological data, several agrivoltaic Amaducci system configurations, and scenarios. The work carried out by et al. (2018) is considered a milestone for the technology since it indicated that agrivoltaic systems can support crop yield, clean energy production, and water saving, thus playing a key role in the energy–food–water nexus. Moreover, the study showed that agrivoltaic systems can improve crop resilience to climate-change- and weather-induced phenomena like drought. No optimisation was set up and performed in Amaducci et al. (2018). More recently, through simulations and sensitivity analysis, Trommsdorff et al. (2021) studied the effect of an agrivoltaic system’s design parameters on solar radiation availability to crops grown underneath the agrivoltaic system. In all the cases and scenarios investigated, the _LER_ exceeded one (i.e., the land productivity, considering both electricity and food production, is higher with agrivoltaic systems than when the same land is employed for mono production). Barron-Gafford et al. (2019) also studied the energy–water–food nexus of agrivoltaic systems. Their results, like those of Amaducci et al. (2018), showed that the combination of _PV_ systems with farm activities could lead to reduced plant drought stress, and higher food yield. Nevertheless, for the first time, through a fully monitored experiment, the authors showed that agrivoltaic systems can reduce _PV_ panel heat stress, leading to higher energy conversion efficiencies. Economic aspects of agrivoltaic systems were studied by Schindele et al. (2020), and by Agostini et al. (2021); nevertheless, those studies were mostly economic assessments of specific existing agrivoltaic systems,

and optimisation was not included.

Agrivoltaic systems are fully embracing the concepts of green economy by promoting low carbon technologies, reducing pollution, using resources efficiently, boosting employment, and preventing loss of agroecosystem services (UNEP, 2021). While the integration of clean energy technologies and reduced greenhouse gas emissions is evident given the exploitation of photovoltaic systems for converting solar energy into electricity, the more efficient use of natural resources under agrivoltaic systems is related to the increased land productivity and water productivity. Parkinson and Hunt (2020) showed that the conversion from irrigated agriculture to rainfed agriculture in combination with agrivoltaics in areas marked out by high groundwater stress could reduce groundwater depletion by about 150 km[3 ] (about 90% of the global total). Agrivoltaic systems allow living conditions in rural areas to be improved in both developed and developing countries by creating job opportunities as well as guaranteeing farmers’ double – and less volatile – revenues. This has the potential to boost the market for large-scale installations on agricultural land with several benefits for employment. For instance, the Italian government has planned to install 1.04 GWp of agrivoltaic systems as a strategy for the post-Covid recovery plan (Italian Government, 2021). Proctor et al. (2021) studied how agrivoltaics align with the Green New Deal resolution (GND) (United States of America House of Representative, 2019) and evaluated that in 20 years agrivoltaics could create 100,000 jobs in the United States of America. Concerning agrosystem services, agrivoltaic systems allow pollinators and biodiversity to be increased with several advantages for agricultural productivity (Graham et al., 2021). The land close to the mounting structure that cannot be used for agriculture – in the order of 10% for vertically mounted agrivoltaic systems – can be used as habitat for pollinators and to increase biodiversity, with positive effects on crop yield productivity (Dainese et al., 2019; Kleijn et al., 2019). D’Amato et al. (2017) provided an in-depth analysis of topics within the concepts of circular economy, green economy, and bio economy. Sustainable development, renewable energy conversion, and land use were among the most emerging topics within green economy. Othman et al. (2018) identified agrivoltaics as one of the pathways for developing the green economy of Malaysia given the economic benefits that the co-existence of electricity production, food production, and improved ecological performances can bring to solar farms. Loiseau et al. (2016) highlighted that innovation is a key requirement for the green economy and that, in this framework, agrivoltaics represent a blank canvas for innovation – including both technical innovation such as mounting structure, software and control system development, and business model development to support the synergies between food and electricity production. Among the technical innovations, Proctor et al. (2021) identified the combination of agrivoltaics and electric tractors as an opportunity to decarbonise the agricultural sector. Among the social benefits of the green economy, the authors listed increased resilience to natural hazard. The technology will allow energy and food systems to be made more resilient during drought and under the most adverse predicted climate changes. This aligns with the experimental results presented by Trommsdorff et al. (2021) in which the highest LER of agrivoltaics was achieved during extreme weather events such as drought, since the shade produced by the photovoltaic modules on the ground reduces water and temperature stresses. In the context of sustainable development, agrivoltaic systems represents a key technology to meet the sustainable development goals, especially zero hunger, clean and affordable energy, and climate action (United Nations, 2021), but also to avoid the deep conflicts among the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The competition between land for energy and land for food in large-scale solar farms is seen as a threat to food security and it creates deep conflicts among the SDGs (i.e., Zero Hunger, Affordable and Clean Energy, and Climate Action) (Brunet et al., 2020). The configuration of utility-scale solar farms into agrivoltaic systems allows those criticisms to be avoided by exploiting the synergies between electricity and food production. Moreover, it also produces a positive effect on the water

consumption from agriculture and related SDG (i.e., Clean Water and Sanitation) as studied by Parkinson and Hunt (2020). Agrivoltaics also configure as an integrated technology that promotes an interdisciplinary approach to address all the interrelationships between food production, electricity production, water consumption, biodiversity, climate adaptation, social, and economic aspects. Multidisciplinarity was defined by Baleta et al. (2019) as a key pathway for reaching the SDGs.

To the best knowledge of the authors, there is a research gap in the field of agrivoltaics related to techno-economic optimisation of systems. Moreover, to the best knowledge of the authors, extremely few research activities have been conducted on agrivoltaic systems in Sweden. Most of the research efforts have been focused on solar irrigation systems (Campana et al., 2015) and integration of _PV_ systems and greenhouses (Vadiee and Martin, 2013). From the report by Lindahl et al. (2020), most applications of _PV_ systems in agriculture are simply related to integrating _PV_ systems on farms buildings. This research gap is mostly due to the interdisciplinarity of the field, with some of the researchers focusing only on crop modelling and other researchers focusing only on _PV_ system modelling. To address this research gap, this study aims to develop an optimisation model for agrivoltaic systems. This is done by leveraging our previous study on the water–food–energy nexus (Campana et al., 2018) and _PV_ system modelling (Campana et al., 2020). The model developed in this study optimises the design parameters of a vertically mounted agrivoltaic system using bifacial _PV_ modules. This agrivoltaic system configuration has been chosen since it is the same technology used in first agrivoltaic system in Sweden as shown in Fig. 1. Beside the aim of developing a robust water–food–energy nexus model for the simulation and optimisation of vertically mounted agrivoltaic systems, this study also aims to answer the following main research questions:

- 1) How does the optimisation of vertical bifacial _PV_ systems affect crop yield and electricity production?

- 2) How are the optimisation results affected by the grown crop?

This study is structured as follows. Section 2 describes the modelling chain and optimisation model with special emphasis on the shading model. Section 3 presents the simulation and optimisation results; the simulation results are also complemented by the Appendix. Section 4 presents the limitations of the current version of the model and the impact of the model results on the agrivoltaic market in Sweden, and discusses potential policy implications. Section 5 summarises the conclusion of this study.

## **2. Modelling and optimisation**

The model calculates _PV_ production, starting from climatological data and applying algorithms concerning solar position, solar decomposition and transposition, and solar shading. Crop yield is calculated by feeding the crop yield model with the effective Photosynthetically Active Radiation ( _PAR_ ), and other key climatological and agricultural parameters. The effective _PAR_ reaching the crop is calculated by considering the diffuse and beam components of the _PAR_ and considering the shadows produced by the bifacial _PV_ modules rows on the ground. The model developed in this study is based on the modelling and optimisation framework of the open-source package OptiCE (OptiCE, 2021; Campana et al., 2017).

## _2.3. Solar decomposition and transposition models_

The diffuse component of the global solar radiation has been retrieved from Strång (2021a), but, due to the unavailability of the diffuse component of the _PAR_ , the _PAR_ decomposition model from Gu et al. (1999) is implemented (Oliphant and Stoy, 2018). The decomposition model calculates the diffuse fraction of the global radiation. The diffuse component of the _PAR_ has been used to calculate the total received _PAR_ by considering the effect of shadings. A validation of the _PAR_ decomposition model is provided in Section 3. The solar transposition algorithm refers to Perez 1990 (Perez et al., 1987, 1990) available in the _PV_LIB_ (Sandia National Laboratories, 2021). The solar transposition algorithm calculates the solar radiation hitting an oriented and tilted surface starting from the global and diffuse components of the horizontal radiation. The ground-reflected albedo radiation, and the total solar radiation on the front and rear side of the bifacial _PV_ modules have been calculated with the models from Martín and Ruiz, (2005), Khan et al. (2017), and Sun et al. (2018).

## _4.1. Comparison with previous studies_

Currently, few research studies have focused on the optimisation of agrivoltaic systems, defined as properly setting up an optimisation

**Fig. 15.** Optimal azimuth angle and distance distributions as compared to annual electricity production (objective 3).

model with specific objective functions and decisional variables, and integrating a crop model. Imran et al. (2020) have proposed an optimisation model for single-axis tracking agrivoltaic systems to better convert solar radiation into electricity by adjusting the tilt angle as a function of the _PAR_ absorbed by the crop. Nevertheless, the optimisation model only focused on one aspect of agrivoltaic systems without considering the crop yield response to _PAR_ and related crop stresses. Riaz et al. (2020) optimised the _PV_ density and tilt angle of agrivoltaic systems based on the required _PAR_ at crop level. Nevertheless, even in this case no crop model was considered. Similarly, several authors have studied the effect of sensitive parameters of an agrivoltaic system by relying on sensitivity analyses and combining the results from different software instead of relying on a single platform.

Concerning the _LER_ results achieved in this study, it is important to note that the implementation of an agrivoltaic system can lead to _LER_ above 1.2, which means 20% more productivity for the same land as compared to the monoculture. Values above 1.5 were reported by Trommsdorff et al. (2021) in Germany, while values above 1.2 were reported by Amaducci et al. (2018) in Italy. The main differences as compared to our results are as follows. First, the results of this study refer to a typical year, while the results presented in Trommsdorff et al. (2021), where the highest _LER_ was achieved, refer to a drought year – when the implementation of agrivoltaic systems can achieve the best performances in terms of _LER_ . Other differences in the results can be attributed to different geographical locations and to the fact that the results presented in Trommsdorff et al. (2021) on the _LER_ are related to crop experimental results rather than crop modelling results. This is further explained in the next section concerning the limitations of the current modelling framework developed in this study, especially those concerning the crop model. Another factor contributing to the low _LER_ can be related to the different photovoltaic system configuration (i.e., system orientation and _PV_ modules density).

## _4.2. Limitations_

One of the limitations of this work is that the optimisation should be carried out considering several years and different crop rotations, since the optimal configuration is crop-dependent, as highlighted in Fig. 13. Nevertheless, this is beyond the scope of this study, which focused mostly on the model development. Multi-year and multi-crop optimisations will be undertaken in future studies. More detailed economic analysis based on comprehensive and lifetime-oriented indicators, such –cost ratio will be as the net present value, payback period, or benefit also carried out in future studies. Most of the objective functions used in this work are technically oriented; more economic and environmentally oriented objective functions will be implemented in the future version of the model. Another limitation of the model has been highlighted in Section 2.5, and it concerns the calculation of the shading area, _Ashading_ . Considering or not considering the grass underneath the _PV_ modules can impact the distribution of _PAR_ at the crop level. The effects of those two scenarios on the _PAR_ distribution between the vertical bifacial _PV_ modules rows are presented in the Appendix. Although the simplification introduced in Section 2.5 can affect the _PAR_ distribution, the impact on the total _PAR_ close to the row is not so significant, assuming the dynamic growth of the grass underneath the _PV_ modules.

One of the major limitations of the model presented in this study is related to the crop model. In the current version of the crop model, the crop yield is related to the amount of intercepted _PAR_ by the crop. _PAR_ interception is in turn related to the leaf area index and its development during the crop growing season (Equation (6)). Under shading conditions, as highlighted in Marrou et al. (2013), crops can adapt by increasing the leaf area index and thus the intercepted _PAR_ , leading to lower crop yield losses as compared to what is estimated in this study. Thus, the results presented in this study and concerning the crop yield can be considered as a worst-case scenario. This also explains why, as compared to other studies based on experimental results, lower _LER_

values were achieved in this study. As highlighted in Weselek et al. (2019) and in Trommsdorff et al. (2021), accurately estimating the crop yield response under the agrivoltaic system shading is one of the main modelling challenges. The results from the first agrivoltaic system in Sweden, presented in Figs. 1–3, will shed light on how crops react under complex shading conditions to further improve the model presented in this study.

## _4.3. Policy implications_

Recently, _PV_ solar park developers in Sweden have claimed to have reached grid parity with the Nord Pool spot price (Nord Pool, 2021). This has led to a dramatic increase in interest in investing in solar parks. As an example, one of the largest solar _PV_ installers in Sweden, Solkompaniet AB, plans to install a 1 GWp solar park in the coming years (Gigawattparken, 2021). However, large-scale solar farms face several challenges with the authorisation and the environmental permission process to access agricultural land (Aspeteg and Bergek, 2020). Moreover, agricultural land is currently considered unsuitable for the construction of utility-scale solar systems (Lindberg et al., 2021). In Section 3.2, the model results in terms of _LER_ show that, in Sweden, agrivoltaic systems have the capability to increase land-use efficiency by at least 20% as compared to monoculture. Moreover, by increasing the unused land as shown in Fig. 3, agrivoltaics have the potential to boost pollinators, biodiversity, and thus crop productivity, as shown in previous research (Dainese et al., 2019; Kleijn et al., 2019). Those aspects can have potential positive effects on the development of policies and regulations that facilitate the permission process for large-scale solar farms, especially if they are configured as agrivoltaic systems. Agrivoltaic systems themselves and solar farms configured as agrivoltaic systems have the potential to significantly boost the _PV_ market in Sweden, with _PV_ installation several benefits to the economy considering the solar supply chain (i.e., solar modules, inverters, other system components, design and permitting process, installation, connection to the grid, maintenance, replacement, and decommissioning) and related job opportunities. In 2019, the estimated full job places per MWp installed capacity were 7.7 in Sweden (Lindahl et al., 2020).

As of 2021, in Sweden, there is only a subsidy scheme for private people that install _PV_ systems. The earlier investment subsidy for companies, including large solar parks, with a maximum of SEK 1.2 million per system (Lindahl et al., 2020) (SEK 1 ≈ EUR 0.1) was closed in July 2020. The electricity certificate scheme that earlier could provide some additional income for solar parks has recently reached its goal in installed renewable power, resulting in a close-to-zero value for these certificates. The value of guarantees of origin is also very low. Therefore, solar parks in Sweden must be developed without any subsidies. – Nevertheless, in the period 2015 19, the agricultural sector has benefited from direct capital subsidy through the European Agricultural Fund for Agricultural Development for _PV_ installations on agricultural buildings. The resulting cumulative installed _PV_ capacity and subsidy were 3.725 MWp and 15.7 MSEK, respectively (Lindahl et al., 2020). The direct capital subsidy was in the order of 40% of total investment cost. This type of subsidy was higher as compared to residential and commercial _PV_ systems since, due to tax regulations, the value of self-consumed electricity is lower for farmers than for residential and commercial _PV_ applications. However, this subsidy was handled differently in different counties, and was not applicable in all counties. As a first stage, since the agrivoltaic sector is a rapidly expanding sector, as a policy measure we could recommend applying the same subsidy scheme for agricultural buildings to small-scale (i.e., lower than 50–100 kWp) experimental agrivoltaic systems to study more in depth the impact that agrivoltaic systems can have on the crop yield for different crops and at different locations. This could be a starting subsidy scheme to gain more in-depth knowledge on the interrelationships between system configuration, and electricity and food production. Such an approach will benefit farmers’ income, self-consumption due to the

limited _PV_ capacity of the agrivoltaic systems and grid-related issues, knowledge, and policies development. It must be pointed out that fastgrowing plantations for energy purposes have also received subsidies (Xu and Mola-Yudego, 2021) despite the energy yield per unit area of such plantations being considerably lower than that of agrivoltaic systems. By way of example, the electricity production per unit area of the agrivoltaic system simulated in Section 3.1 is about 30 kWh/m[2] /year while the average annual net energy yield for willow production at high nitrogen fertilisation is 175 GJ/ha/year (Nordborg et al., 2018) which is equivalent to about 4.86 kWh/m[2] /year. It must also be pointed out that, as compared to countries like Japan, Italy, and Germany, where policies for supporting agrivoltaic systems have already been developed or are under development, there is not yet any agrivoltaic systems policy or regulation or agrivoltaic system definition on the Swedish Government agenda. The motivation of having a subsidy scheme can be explained by analysing the key factors that drive the installation of solar photovoltaic systems. As pointed out in Colasante et al. (2021) for Italy, self-consumption and the related lowering of energy bills and cost-competitiveness are key factors in the desire to install solar _PV_ systems. Similar results were pointed out in Mundaca and Samahita (2020) for Sweden. The authors identified subsidies and peer effect as key factors for the adoption of distributed solar _PV_ systems. Despite it is beyond the scope of this work of analysing such mechanisms, the alardalen  ̈ Uni- installation of the first agrivoltaic system in Sweden (M versity, 2021) has attracted several media coverage in which both re– searchers and farmer involved in the project explained the benefits both technical and economic – and challenges of the systems. This has boosted the interest of several other farmers in knowing more and installing other small-to large-scale agrivoltaic systems. In most of the meetings, farmers pointed out the possibility of support from capital subsidies directly from the government as well as from research funding. This aligns with the findings of Mundaca and Samahita (2020).

In a second stage, after the impacts of different agrivoltaic systems configurations are well known on different crops and at different geographical locations, the Swedish Government could start to support larger-scale agrivoltaic systems through capital investment subsidies or through feed-in tariffs, to stimulate the market and facilitate the technology/system adoption. Moreover, it must be pointed out that, since agrivoltaic systems bridge agricultural and energy sectors, different ministries should be involved in the process to decide on subsidies and to coordinate both agricultural and energy subsidies. In addition, it is worth mentioning that the most advanced policies on agrivoltaic systems, for instance in Japan, allow subsidies to be released for agrivoltaic systems only if the crop reduction under the agrivoltaic systems system is lower than 20% (Trommsdorff et al., 2021). Defining the crop yield reduction at the planning stage cannot be performed without a robust model that can accurately simulate the synergies between agrivoltaic system design, _PV_ module densities, shadings, and crop yield. This study aims to fill this research and market gap. It is also suggested that, in the second stage, the authorisation process for large-scale solar photovoltaic farms could be facilitated if those are configured as agrivoltaic systems to minimise the impact on food production.

- The agrivoltaic model presented in this study is composed of several sub-models. In particular, the models concerning shadings, _PAR_ decomposition, crop yield, and _PV_ production model are the most fundamental. The validation of those sub-models shows the robustness of the model in identifying the interrelationships between crop productivity and electricity production based on the system configuration (i.e., orientation and row distance).

- The row distance significantly affects the _PAR_ distribution and, at the latitude of the investigated location, crop yield can be almost halved by changing from 20 m to 5 m distance between mutual rows.

- By analysing the optimisation results, the _LER_ cannot be used as a main parameter for the optimal design of agrivoltaic systems. More objective functions should be included for a better estimation of the synergies between crop and electricity production. Maximising the _LER_ tends to drastically reduce electricity production, and this could undermine the investment in the _PV_ system, or vice versa it could lead to crop failure.

- By studying the contributions of _LER_ for a specific year (i.e., the crop yield and the electricity production contributions), it is evident that the optimal row distance varies according to the crop (i.e., 9.7 m for potato and 9.2 m for oats) and this leads to important consequences in terms of the long-term optimal design of an agrivoltaic system. This should consider multi-year and multi-crop simulations and optimisation based on conventional farm activities.

- The implementation of an agrivoltaic system for the investigated crops and locations shows a _LER_ above 1.2, as also estimated in previous studies conducted in Germany and Italy. These results justify the implementation of agrivoltaic systems to meet green economy and sustainability goals.
